note.question: Are agents indeed hurt by an expansion in the labor pool size?
note.overview: An on-demand service platform relies on independent workers (agents) who decide how much time, if any, to devote to the platform. Some labor advocates have argued that an expansion of the labor pool hurts agents—by reducing the wage and agent utilization (i.e., the fraction of time an agent is busy serving customers). Motivated by concern for agent welfare, regulators are considering measures that reduce the labor pool size or that impose a floor on the nominal wage or effective wage (i.e., the product of the nominal wage and agent utilization).

Methodology: We employ an equilibrium model that accounts for the interaction among price, wage, labor supply, customer delay, and demand.

Contrary to the conventional view that consumers are hurt by an effective wage floor (because they face a higher price, due to upward pressure on the wage, and longer delay, due to upward pressure on agent utilization), consumers actually benefit.
The opportunity cost for an agent is ax2, where a denotes the agent’s opportunity cost parameter.

We assume that the amount of work an agent receives is proportional to the amount of time the agent makes himself available through the platform;3 that is, an agent who decides to make himself available for time x receives an amount of work equal to x S D, where S is the labor supply (the cumulative amount of time from all the agents per unit of time) and D is the demand (also measured in per unit of time).

A customer with a need seeks service if her utility from doing so, v −p −hW, is nonnegative, where v is the customer’s valuation, p is the price, W is a measure of delay, and h > 0 is the customer’s delay sensitivity (i.e., cost per unit of time delayed).

Our choice of delay measure (4) is consistent with the observation from the queueing literature that in many congested systems, delay is a function of both the difference S −D and the ratio D/S (i.e., utilization).
